text.title: NDA / MSA Obligation Extractor Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules with rationale + source for nda-msa-obligation-extractor. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Each obligation MUST carry: obligation_id, source (contract section), text excerpt, owner, trigger, deadline, evidence pointer, status.
rule.rationale: An obligation recorded as a paragraph of prose cannot be operated on: no reader can tell from it who has to act, what starts the clock, or what would count as having complied. Fixing the fields converts each of those unknowns into an empty cell, which is a finding someone can be asked to close. The same gap inside prose is invisible and survives untouched to the audit.

rule.statement: Every obligation MUST cite the contract section (e.g. 'MSA §4.2') and the verbatim text excerpt; paraphrase-only obligations are forbidden.
rule.rationale: A paraphrase is an interpretation, and once it enters the register the team complies with the interpretation rather than with the agreement; where the two diverge, only the executed document counts. Carrying the section reference and the verbatim words lets any reader re-check the reading against the instrument instead of trusting the extractor, and it is what makes re-mapping possible when an amendment rewrites the underlying clause.

rule.statement: Each obligation MUST have a single named owner; co-ownership ('legal + delivery') is forbidden as it diffuses accountability.
rule.rationale: Shared ownership fails in a specific way: neither owner refuses the obligation, each assumes the other holds it, and nothing happens until the breach surfaces. A single name matters less for blame afterwards than for the moment of assignment, when exactly one person has to notice they are now carrying it and either accept or push back. A pairing like "legal plus delivery" produces no such moment for anyone.

rule.statement: Trigger MUST be expressed as an observable condition (date, event, threshold); 'as needed' triggers are forbidden because they never fire.
rule.rationale: A trigger phrased as "as needed" depends on somebody noticing the right moment, and noticing is exactly the faculty that fails under delivery pressure, which is why the recurring symptom is "we did not realise we owed that". An observable condition can be wired to a calendar entry or a monitor, and it can be shown after the fact to have been met or not met, which a judgement call can never be.

rule.statement: Deadline MUST be ISO date or explicit 'continuous' / 'on-trigger'; missing deadline blocks the register.
rule.rationale: An obligation with no deadline can never be overdue, so it never appears on an exception report and is structurally invisible to every review that follows. Requiring "continuous" or "on-trigger" as explicit values is what separates "this genuinely has no date" from "nobody has worked the date out yet", because both otherwise render as the same blank cell, and a blank is always read as the harmless one.

rule.statement: Each obligation MUST point to where the evidence of compliance lives (file path, ticket id, calendar reminder); orphan obligations are auto-flagged.
rule.rationale: Complying and being able to demonstrate compliance are separate problems, and only the second is testable by a client auditor or usable in a dispute. Evidence captured as the work happens costs almost nothing; reconstructed a year later out of memory and chat history it is expensive and frequently impossible. An obligation with nowhere for evidence to land is also a reliable tell that nobody has yet worked out how it will actually be met, which is why the orphans are worth flagging on their own.

rule.statement: Register reviewed quarterly; new obligations triggered by amendments are added; expired obligations are archived with date.
rule.rationale: The register is a snapshot of a document that keeps moving: amendments, new statements of work and renewals both add obligations and retire them. Left unreviewed it drifts into something the team still trusts but that no longer matches the agreement, which is worse than having no register, because it gets consulted instead of the instrument. Archiving expired entries with their date rather than deleting them preserves the answer an auditor actually asks for, which is what applied at the time.

rule.statement: Sharing the register beyond the engagement team MUST redact verbatim contract excerpts unless legal cleared the share.
rule.rationale: The register concentrates the parts of the agreement the counterparty most wants controlled, and confidentiality clauses commonly cover the terms of the agreement itself, so circulating the tool built to keep you compliant can be the breach it exists to prevent. Redacting the verbatim excerpts still leaves the operational fields, which is all a wider audience needs; the exact wording is only required by the few people who have to interpret it.

rule.statement: If the engagement contract has fewer than 10 operational obligations, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Extraction cost is close to fixed per contract, so below a handful of operational obligations the register costs more than the tracking it replaces, which the delivery lead can hold in working memory. A register also creates its own upkeep burden and, once it exists, an assumption of coverage, so a thin one built for the sake of completeness ends up asserting more diligence than was actually applied.
